readings.c1s1:
¶
'''aboriginality''' (ab-ọ-rij-i-nal′i-ti), ''n.'' The quality or state of being aboriginal. ''N. E. D.''

'''aboriginally''' (ab-ō-rij′i-nal-i), ''adv.'' In an aboriginal manner; originally; from the very first.
{{smaller block|There are hardly any domestic races . . . which have not been ranked . . . as the descendants of ''aboriginally'' distinct species.
{{right|''Darwin'', Origin of Species, p. 16.}}}}

'''aboriginary''' (ab-ō-rij′i-nạ̄-ri), ''n.'' An aboriginal inhabitant. ''N. E. D.''

'''ab origine''' (ab ō-rij′i-nē). [L.: ''ab'', from; ''origine'', abl. of ''origo'', origin.] From the origin, beginning, or start.

'''aborigine''' (ab-ọ-rij′i-nē), ''n.'' [Sing. from L. pl. ''aborigines'', as if the latter were an E. word.] One of the aborigines (which see); an aboriginal. Also called ''aborigen'', ''aborigin''.

'''aborigines''' (ab-ō-rij′i-nēz), ''n. pl.'' [L., pl., the first inhabitants, applied especially to the aboriginal inhabitants of Latium, the ancestors of the Roman people, < ''ab'', from, + ''origo'' (''origin-''), origin, beginning.] '''1.''' The primitive inhabitants of a country; the people living in a country at the earliest period of which anything is known.—'''2.''' The original fauna and flora of a given geographical area.

'''aborsement†''' (ạ-bôrs′ment), ''n.'' [< L. ''aborsus'', brought forth prematurely (collateral form of ''abortus'': see ''abort'', ''v.''), + ''-ment''.] Abortion. ''Bp. Hall.''

'''aborsive†''' (ạ-bôr′siv), ''a.'' [< L. ''aborsus'', collateral form of ''abortus'' (see ''abort'', ''v.''), + E. ''-ive''.]
readings.c1s2:
Abortive; premature. ''Fuller.''

'''abort''' (a-bôrt′), ''v. i.'' [< L. ''abortare'', miscarry, < ''abortus'', pp. of ''aboriri'', miscarry, fail, < ''ab'', from, away, + ''oriri'', arise, grow.] '''1.''' To miscarry in giving birth.—'''2.''' To become aborted or abortive; appear or remain in a rudimentary or undeveloped state: as, organs liable to ''abort''.
{{smaller block|In the pelagic Phyllirhöe, the foot ''aborts'', as well as the mantle, and the body has the form of an elongated sac.
{{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Invert., p. 438.}}
The temperature now falls, and the disease [smallpox] in some cases will ''abort'' at this stage [at the end of forty-eight hours].
{{right|''Quain'', Med. Dict., p. 1442.}}}}

'''abort†''' (ạ-bôrt′), ''n.'' [< L. ''abortus'', an abortion, miscarriage, < ''abortus'', pp. of ''aboriri'': see ''abort'', ''v.''] An abortion. ''Burton.''

'''aborted''' (ạ-bôr′ted), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Brought forth before its time.—'''2.''' Imperfectly developed; incapable of discharging its functions; not having acquired its functions.
{{smaller block|Although the eyes of the Cirripeds are more or less ''aborted'' in their mature state, they retain sufficient susceptibility of light to excite retraction of the cirri.
{{right|''Owen'', Comp. Anat., xiii.}}}}

'''aborticide''' (ạ-bôr′ti-sīd), ''n.'' [< L. ''abortus'' (see ''abort'', ''n.'') + ''-cidium'' (as in ''homicidium'', homicide<sup>1</sup>), < ''cædere'', kill.] In ''obstet.'', the destruction of a fetus in the uterus; feticide.

'''abortient''' (ạ-bôr′shiẹnt), ''a.'' [< LL. ''abortien(t-)s'', ppr. of ''abortire'', miscarry, equiv. to ''abortare'': see ''abort'', ''v.''] In ''bot.'', sterile; barren.

'''abortifacient''' (ạ-bôr-ti-fā′shiẹnt), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''abortus'' (see ''abort'', ''n.'') + ''facien(t-)s'', ppr. of ''facere'', make.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Producing abortion:

<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="proofreader" />{{RunningHeader|aboriginality|16|about}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''aboriginality''' (ab-ọ-rij-i-nal′i-ti), ''n.'' The quality or state of being aboriginal.  ''N. E. D.''

'''aboriginally''' (ab-ō-rij′i-nal-i), ''adv.'' In an aboriginal manner; originally; from the very first.
{{smaller block|There are hardly any domestic races . . . which have not been ranked . . . as the descendants of ''aboriginally'' distinct species.
{{right|''Darwin'', Origin of Species, p. 16.}}}}

'''aboriginary''' (ab-ō-rij′i-nạ̄-ri), ''n.'' An aboriginal inhabitant.  ''N. E. D.''

'''ab origine''' (ab ō-rij′i-nē).  [L.: ''ab'', from; ''origine'', abl. of ''origo'', origin.]  From the origin, beginning, or start.

'''aborigine''' (ab-ọ-rij′i-nē), ''n.''  [Sing. from L. pl. ''aborigines'', as if the latter were an E. word.]  One of the aborigines (which see); an aboriginal. Also called ''aborigen'', ''aborigin''.

'''aborigines''' (ab-ō-rij′i-nēz), ''n. pl.''  [L., pl., the first inhabitants, applied especially to the aboriginal inhabitants of Latium, the ancestors of the Roman people, < ''ab'', from, + ''origo'' (''origin-''), origin, beginning.]  '''1.''' The primitive inhabitants of a country; the people living in a country at the earliest period of which anything is known.—'''2.''' The original fauna and flora of a given geographical area.

'''aborsement†''' (ạ-bôrs′ment), ''n.''  [< L. ''aborsus'', brought forth prematurely (collateral form of ''abortus'': see ''abort'', ''v.''), + ''-ment''.]  Abortion.  ''Bp. Hall.''

'''aborsive†''' (ạ-bôr′siv), ''a.''  [< L. ''aborsus'', collateral form of ''abortus'' (see ''abort'', ''v.''), + E. ''-ive''.]  Abortive; premature.  ''Fuller.''

'''abort''' (a-bôrt′), ''v. i.''  [< L. ''abortare'', miscarry, < ''abortus'', pp. of ''aboriri'', miscarry, fail, < ''ab'', from, away, + ''oriri'', arise, grow.]  '''1.''' To miscarry in giving birth.—'''2.''' To become aborted or abortive; appear or remain in a rudimentary or undeveloped state: as, organs liable to ''abort''.
{{smaller block|In the pelagic Phyllirhöe, the foot ''aborts'', as well as the mantle, and the body has the form of an elongated sac.
{{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Invert., p. 438.}}}}
{{smaller block|The temperature now falls, and the disease [smallpox] in some cases will ''abort'' at this stage [at the end of forty-eight hours].
{{right|''Quain'', Med. Dict., p. 1442.}}}}

'''abort†''' (ạ-bôrt′), ''n.''  [< L. ''abortus'', an abortion, miscarriage, < ''abortus'', pp. of ''aboriri'': see ''abort'', ''v.'']  An abortion.  ''Burton.''

'''aborted''' (ạ-bôr′ted), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Brought forth before its time.—'''2.''' Imperfectly developed; incapable of discharging its functions; not having acquired its functions.
{{smaller block|Although the eyes of the Cirripeds are more or less ''aborted'' in their mature state, they retain sufficient susceptibility of light to excite retraction of the cirri.
{{right|''Owen'', Comp. Anat., xiii.}}}}

'''aborticide''' (ạ-bôr′ti-sīd), ''n.''  [< L. ''abortus'' (see ''abort'', ''n.'') + ''-cidium'' (as in ''homicidium'', homicide<sup>1</sup>), < ''cædere'', kill.]  In ''obstet.'', the destruction of a fetus in the uterus; feticide.

'''abortient''' (ạ-bôr′shiẹnt), ''a.''  [< LL. ''abortien(t-)s'', ppr. of ''abortire'', miscarry, equiv. to ''abortare'': see ''abort'', ''v.'']  In ''bot.'', sterile; barren.

'''abortifacient''' (ạ-bôr-ti-fā′shiẹnt), ''a.'' and ''n.''  [< L. ''abortus'' (see ''abort'', ''n.'') + ''facien(t-)s'', ppr. of ''facere'', make.]  '''I.''' ''a.'' Producing abortion: said of drugs and operative procedures.

'''II.''' ''n.'' In ''med.'', whatever is or may be used to produce abortion.
{{smaller block|The almost universal keeping of ''abortifacients'' by druggists, despite statutes to the contrary.
{{right|''N. Y. Independent'', July 24, 1873.}}}}

'''abortion''' (a̤-bôr′shọn), ''n.''  [< L. ''abortio(n-)'', miscarriage, < ''aboriri'', miscarry: see ''abort'', ''v.'']  '''1.''' Miscarriage; the expulsion of the fetus before it is viable — that is, in women, before about the 28th week of gestation. {{smaller|Expulsion of the fetus occurring later than this, but before the normal time, is called (when not procured by art, as by a surgical operation) ''premature labor''. A somewhat useless distinction has been sometimes drawn between ''abortion'' and ''miscarriage'', by which the former is made to refer to the first four months of pregnancy and the latter to the following three months. ''Criminal abortion'' is premeditated or intentional abortion procured, at any period of pregnancy, by artificial means, and solely for the purpose of preventing the birth of a living child; feticide. At common law the criminality depended on the abortion being caused after quickening. Some modern statutes provide otherwise.}}
{{smaller block|In the penitential discipline of the Church, ''abortion'' was placed in the same category as infanticide, and the stern sentences to which the guilty person was subject imprinted on the minds of Christians, more deeply than any mere exhortations, a sense of the enormity of the crime.
{{right|''Lecky'', Europ. Morals, II. 24.}}}}
'''2.''' The product of untimely birth; hence, a misshapen being; a monster. — '''3.''' Any fruit or product that does not come to maturity; hence, frequently, in a figurative sense, anything which fails in its progress before it is matured or perfected, as a design or project.—'''4.''' In ''bot.'' and ''zoöl.'', the arrested development of an organ at a more or less early stage.
{{smaller block|In the complete ''abortion'' of the rostellum [of ''Cephalanthera grandiflora''] we have evidence of degradation.
{{right|''Darwin'', Fertil. of Orchids by Insects, p. 80.}}}}
{{smaller block|He [Mr. Bates] claims for that family [the ''Heliconidæ''] the highest position, chiefly because of the imperfect structure of the fore legs, which is there carried to an extreme degree of ''abortion.''
{{right|''A. R. Wallace'', Nat. Selec., p. 133.}}}}

'''abortional''' (a̤-bôr′shọn-a̤l), ''a.'' Of the nature of an abortion; characterized by failure.
{{smaller block|The treaty . . . proved ''abortional'', and never came to fulfilment. {{right|''Carlyle'', Frederick the Great, VI. xv. 22.}}}}

'''abortionist''' (a̤-bôr′shọn-ist), ''n.''  [< ''abortion'' + ''-ist.'']  One who produces or aims to produce a criminal abortion; especially, one who makes a practice of so doing.
{{smaller block|He [Dr. Robb] urged the necessity of physicians using all their influence to discountenance the work of ''abortionists.'' {{right|''N. Y. Med. Jour.'', XL. 580.}}}}

'''abortive''' (a̤-bôr′tiv), ''a.'' and ''n.''  [< L. ''abortivus'', born prematurely, causing abortion, < ''abortus'', pp. of ''aboriri'', miscarry: see ''abort, v.'']  '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Brought forth in an imperfect condition; imperfectly formed or inadequately developed, as an animal or vegetable production; rudimentary.—'''2.''' Suppressed; kept imperfect; remaining rudimentary, or not advancing to perfection in form or function: a frequent use of the term in zoölogy. Compare ''vestigial.''
{{smaller block|The toes [of seals] are completely united by strong webs, and the straight nails are sometimes reduced in number, or even altogether ''abortive''. {{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Vert., p. 359.}}}}
{{smaller block|The power of voluntarily uncovering the canine [tooth] on one side of the face being thus often wholly lost, indicates that it is a rarely used and almost ''abortive'' action.
{{right|''Darwin'', Express. of Emot., p. 253.}}}}
Hence —'''3.''' Not brought to completion or to a successful issue; failing; miscarrying; coming to nought: as, an ''abortive'' scheme.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Abortive'' as the first-born bloom of spring,
Nipp’d with the lagging rear of winter’s frost.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 1576.}}}}
{{smaller block|He made a salutation, or, to speak nearer the truth, an ill-defined, ''abortive'' attempt at courtesy.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, vii.}}}}
'''4.''' In ''bot.'', defective; barren.  ''A. Gray.''—'''5.''' Producing nothing; chaotic; ineffectual.
{{smaller block|<poem>{{gap}}{{gap}}The void profound
Of unessential Night receives him next,
Wide-gaping; and with utter loss of being
Threatens him, plunged in that ''abortive'' gulf.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 438.}}}}
'''6.''' In ''med.'', producing or intended to produce abortion; abortifacient: as, ''abortive'' drugs.—'''7.''' Deformed; monstrous. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou elvish-mark’d, ''abortive'', rooting hog!
Thou that wast seal’d in thy nativity
The slave of nature and the son of hell!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 3.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Abortive vellum''', vellum made from the skin of a still-born calf.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' [< L. ''abortivum'', an abortion, abortive medicine; neut. of ''abortivus'', a.: see the adj.] '''1.''' That which is produced prematurely; an abortion; a monstrous birth.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Abortives'', presages, and tongues of heaven.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 4.}}}} '''2.''' A drug causing abortion; an abortifacient.

'''abortive†''' (a̤-bôr′tiv), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''trans.'' To cause to fail or miscarry.
{{smaller block|He wrought to ''abortive'' the bill before it came to the birth.
{{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, i. 148.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To fail; perish; come to nought.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus one of your bold thunders may ''abortive'',
And cause that birth miscarry.</poem>
{{right|''Tomkis'' (?), Albumazar, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|When peace came so near to the birth, how it ''abortived'', and by whose fault, come now to be remembered.
{{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, ii. 147.}}}}

'''abortively''' (a̤-bôr′tiv-li), ''adv.'' In an abortive or untimely manner; prematurely; imperfectly; ineffectually; as an abortion.
{{smaller block|<poem>{{gap}}If ''abortively'' poor man must die,
Nor reach what reach he might, why die in dread?</poem>
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, vii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The enterprise in Ireland, as elsewhere, terminated ''abortively''.
{{right|''Froude'', Hist. Eng., IV. 94.}}}}

'''abortiveness''' (a̤-bôr′tiv-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being, or of tending to become, abortive; a failure to reach perfection or maturity; want of success or accomplishment.

'''abortment†''' (a-bôrt′ment), ''n.''  [< ''abort'', ''v.'', + ''-ment'', = F. ''avortement'', Sp. ''abortamiento'', Pg. ''abortamento''.]  An untimely birth; an abortion.
{{smaller block|The earth, in whose womb those deserted mineral riches must ever lie buried as lost ''abortments''.
{{right|''Bacon'', Phys. and Med. Remains.}}}}

'''abortus''' (a̤-bôr′tus), ''n.''; pl. ''abortus.''  [L., an abortion: see ''abort, n.'']  In ''med.'', the fruit of an abortion; a child born before the proper time; an abortion.

'''Abothrophera''' (a-both-rof′ẹ-rä̤), ''n. pl.''  [NL., prop. *''abothrophora'', < Gr. ἀ- priv. + βόθρος, a pit, + -φόρος, < φέρειν = E. ''bear''<sup>1</sup>.]  A group of old-world solenoglyph venomous serpents, corresponding to the family ''Viperidæ.'' {{smaller|So called because of the absence of a pit between the eyes and nose, contrasting in this respect with the ''Bothrophera.''}}

'''abought†''', pret. of ''aby.''  [See ''aby.'']  Endured; atoned for; paid dearly for.
{{smaller block|<poem>{{gap}}The vengeans of thilke yre
That Atheon ''aboughte'' trewely.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1445.}}}}

'''aboulia, aboulomania''', ''n.'' Same as ''abulia.''

'''abound''' (a̤-bound′), ''v. i.''  [< ME. ''abounden, abunden,'' sometimes spelled ''habunden'', < OF. ''abonder, habonder,'' F. ''abonder'' = Sp. Pg. ''abundar'' = It. ''abbondare'', < L. ''abundare'', overflow, < ''ab'', from, away, + ''undare'', rise in waves, overflow, < ''unda'', a wave: see ''undulate.'' Cf. ''redound, surround.'']  '''1.''' To be in great plenty; be very prevalent.
{{smaller block|Where sin ''abounded'', grace did much more ''abound.''
{{right|Rom. v. 20.}}}}
{{smaller block|In every political party, in the Cabinet itself, duplicity and perfidy ''abounded.'' {{right|''Macaulay'', Hallam’s Const. Hist.}}}}
'''2.''' To be unstinted in possession or supply (of anything); be copiously provided or furnished (with anything). {{smaller|(''a'') To be rich or affluent (''in''), as that which is a special property or characteristic, or constitutes an individual distinction: as, he ''abounds in''}} wealth or ''in'' charity.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nature ''abounds in'' wits of every kind,
And for each author can a talent find.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Art of Poetry, i. 13.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To teem or be replete (''with''), as that which is furnished or supplied, or is an intrinsic characteristic: as, the country ''abounds with'' wealth, or ''with'' fine scenery.}}
{{smaller block|The faithful man shall ''abound with'' blessings.
{{right|Prov. xxviii. 20.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To abound in''' or '''with one’s own sense†''', to be at liberty to hold or follow one’s own opinion or judgment.}}
{{smaller block|I meddle not with Mr. Ross, but leave him to ''abound in his own sense.'' {{right|''Bramhall'', ii. 632.}}}}
{{smaller block|Moreover, as every one is said to ''abound with his own sense'', and that among the race of man-kind, Opinions and Fancies are found to be as various as the severall Faces and Voyces; so in each individual man there is a differing facultie of Observation, of Judgement, of Application.
{{right|''Howell'', Forreine Travell, i.}}}}

'''aboundance†''' (a̤-boun′da̤ns), ''n.'' An old form of ''abundance. Time’s Storehouse'', ii.

'''abounding''' (a̤-boun′ding), ''n.''  [Verbal n. of ''abound.'']  The state of being abundant; abundance; increase.  ''South'', Sermons, II. 220.

'''abounding''' (a̤-boun′ding), ''p. a.'' Overflowing; plentiful; abundant: as, ''abounding'' wealth.

'''about''' (a̤-bout′), ''adv.'' and ''prep.''  [< ME. ''about, aboute'', earlier ''abouten, abute, abuten'', < AS. ''ābūtan'' (= OFries. ''ābūta''), about, around, < ''ā-'' for ''on'' (the AS. form ''onbūtan'' also occurs, with an equiv. ''ymbūtan'', round about, < ''ymbe, ymb'', around, about, = G. ''um'' = Gr. ἀμφί: see ''amphi-'') + ''būtan'', outside, < ''be'', by, + ''ūtan'', outside, from without, < ''ūt'', prep. and adv., out: see ''on'', ''by'', ''be-''<sup>2</sup>, and ''out''.]  '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' Around; in circuit; circularly; round and round; on every side; in every direction; all around.
{{smaller block|Prithee, do not turn me ''about''; my stomach is not constant.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Algiers . . . measures barely one league ''about''.
{{right|''J. Morgan'', Hist. Algiers.}}}}
'''2.''' Circuitously; in a roundabout course.
{{smaller block|God led the people ''about'' through the way of the wilderness.
{{right|Ex. xiii. 18.}}}}
{{smaller block|To wheel three or four miles ''about''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., i. 6.}}}}
'''3.''' Hither and thither; to and fro; up and down; here and there.
{{smaller block|He that goeth ''about'' as a tale-bearer.
{{right|Prov. xx. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|Wandering ''about'' from house to house.
{{right|1 Tim. v. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|We followed the guide ''about'' among the tombs for a while.
{{right|''C. D. Warner'', Roundabout Journey, xii.}}}}
'''4.''' Near in time, number, quantity, quality, or degree; nearly; approximately; almost.
{{smaller block|He went out ''about'' the third hour.
{{right|Mat. xx. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Light travels ''about'' 186,000 miles a second.
{{right|''J. N. Lockyer'', Elem. Astron.}}}}
{{smaller block|The first two are ''about'' the nicest girls in all London.
{{right|''Hawley Smart'', Social Sinners, I. 182.}}}}
{{smaller block|[In contracts made on the New York Stock Exchange, the term ''about'' means “not more than three days” when applied to time, and “not more than 10 per cent.” when used with reference to a number of shares.]}}
'''5.''' In readiness; intending; going: after the verb ''to be''.
{{smaller block|The house which I am ''about'' to build.
{{right|2 Chron. ii. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|As the shipmen were ''about'' to flee out of the ship.
{{right|Acts xxvii. 30.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
